summary:
Leningrad oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed by President Putin; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are both banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. The note sets out the penalties attached to the 'gay propaganda' statute: public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punished with fines or detention of up to 15 days, and a repeated offence risks criminal prosecution carrying up to four years' imprisonment. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and the note counts at least 139 people in Russia affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and 'extremism' prosecutions.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols. A further 81 people in 98 court cases since January 2024 have been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 'gay propaganda' law.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk in Siberia, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office note (v2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia on account of the extremist designation, and foreign state advisories now name LGBT travellers as a specific risk category rather than a general one.

The legal architecture the oblast inherits did not begin with the 2023 measures. Human Rights Watch traces the current extremism prosecutions back to the 2013 'gay propaganda' law, and the Supreme Court's 2023 designation converted conduct already attracting administrative fines into criminal exposure with a 12-year ceiling.

Criminalisation is partial rather than total: same-sex sexual activity is lawful, while the prohibitions fall on public expression, on legal gender recognition, on marriage, and on gender-affirming care. The same-sex marriage ban bears on visitors travelling with a partner whose relationship Russia will not recognise.

Raids and extremism charges are not confined to the capital. A St Petersburg resident described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation, indicating that the enforcement climate reaches the city nearest to Leningrad oblast.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Leningrad oblast-specific enforcement records, police operations or court outcomes are sourced in this inventory. All convictions, raids and fines cited here are national figures or cases recorded in Moscow, St Petersburg and the Novosibirsk area; whether oblast-level police have carried out comparable raids is unresolved.

The conversion-therapy account concerns a centre near Novosibirsk, not Leningrad oblast, and is presented as evidence that such coercion is documented within Russia rather than as a local finding.

Whether the oblast hosts functioning support services, safe venues or document-change assistance is not sourced, and neither is whether the UK or US advisories name the oblast separately from Russia as a whole.

The UK Home Office note is version 2.0 dated June 2025, with a recorded page update of 12 August 2026; whether later revisions change the figures cited is unresolved.
